owner_rules: Done means ALL evidence: implemented as specified (task id), a test that FAILED before and passes now, suites green, measured number vs target, docs regenerated, committed AND pushed to main.

tasks.title: One command from nothing to a vouched role the receiver can trust
tasks.description: `agentkey setup <role> --principal <id> [--trust <dir>] [--ssh-key <path>] [--json]` does in one step what the flow in the README does in three: creates the role's key if it does not exist, binds it to the person's SSH key, and writes the role's public key into the trust directory the receiver reads (default ./trust), printing the kid, the principal and the one line the agent needs to sign. It refuses to finish with any of the three missing and names the missing piece; it never overwrites an existing key or binding. Proofline's guided setup calls it for the owner role and the agent role. --ssh-key defaults to the key bind already uses (~/.ssh/id_ed25519) so a caller can pass the key it found; --json prints {role, kid, principal, trust, sign} and that shape is the interface proofline reads. Beside <role>.pub the trust directory receives the binding files (<role>.pub.sshsig, <role>.pub.principal) and the principal's allowed_signers line, so the receiver holds the key and what ties it to a person.

criteria.statement: setup in an empty HOME creates the key, the binding and the trust directory files (<role>.pub, <role>.pub.sshsig, <role>.pub.principal, allowed_signers) in one run; the receiver side then works end to end: agentkey verify --keys <trust> verifies an envelope the role signed and verifyBinding on the trust directory copy reads bound; a second run leaves every file under HOME and the trust directory identical in bytes and mtime

tasks.title: Review findings on setup and the interop workflow: six refusals that were silent
tasks.description: Six findings from an automated review of 8583e53 and 2be84bd, each recorded as an issue. The interop workflow (and the release workflow) read the runner label from a repository variable with no fallback, so a repository without the variable cannot run the job. setup reused a role's public key without checking that its private key exists and matches; it checked the trust directory's root for writability and left three copied files behind when allowed_signers turned out to be a directory; it accepted principals that OpenSSH reads as a comment, a list, an invalid entry or a pattern (a * or ? in the field makes the line accept other identities); it reported a trust conflict by comparing bytes, so the raw base64url form of the same key was refused with two identical kids printed; and it decided whether a terminal can ask for a passphrase by opening /dev/tty, which Windows lacks. Each fix carries a test that fails on the code as it is and passes after; bind and setup apply the same principal rule. The release workflow gets the same runner fallback inside AK-06, whose scope covers .github/**; this task fixes the interop workflow and adds the test over every workflow.

criteria.statement: every workflow under .github/workflows that reads a runner label from a variable falls back to ubuntu-latest, and a test refuses one that does not
setup refuses a role public key whose private key is missing or does not match it, and writes nothing
setup preflights every trust destination before the first write and rolls back every file it created when a later step fails; a second run after the obstacle is removed succeeds

a principal that cannot form a single exact allowed_signers entry is refused by setup and by bind before anything is written: the field is a pattern list, so beyond a leading #, a comma, a quote, a leading - and whitespace, the wildcards * and ? are refused too (measured: "a*b" verifies and "*@example.com" would accept other identities); the accepted set is [A-Za-z0-9._@+-], and the binding of an accepted principal verifies
a trust public key in the raw base64url form with the same kid is accepted as the same key; a different kid is still refused
the terminal decision uses the tty flags with the /dev/tty probe as the POSIX fallback, and answers correctly for a Windows and a POSIX environment

tasks.title: Agent identity: honest model, agent-mediated signing, rotation
tasks.description: README and docs state the identity model exactly: a role key identifies the user's role-specific key on that machine, not a unique agent process; every process of that user can read it; isolation options are listed with what each gives. Implemented: AGENTKEY_SIGNER=ssh-agent, where the role key is loaded into ssh-agent with per-use confirmation (`ssh-add -c`) so a signature needs a human confirmation and the private key never sits readable on disk; AGENTKEY_SIGNER=file remains the default and the receipt records `signer: file|ssh-agent|keyless`. Documented option: one OS user per agent with its own AGENTKEY_HOME, and hardware-backed keys via ssh-agent with an `ed25519-sk` token (signatures then verify through ssh-keygen -Y, recorded as signer: sk). Rotation: `agentkey rotate <role>` creates a new key, signs a rotation statement with the old key (old kid, new kid, date) stored in rotations/, sets not_after on the old key; verifiers that know the old kid accept the new one through the chain; hivevault keys trust imports rotation statements with `keys rotate`. Revocation and not_after as in AK-03.

criteria.statement: ssh-agent signer signs through the agent with a confirmation hook and the receipt records signer: ssh-agent; file signer records signer: file
rotate produces a chained statement; a verifier with the old kid accepts the new kid; the old key expires

tasks.title: Expiry is judged at the signature's trusted time, not the verifier's clock
tasks.description: Review (4), agentkey findings, Medium cli.mjs:136: "Expiry is judged at verify time, so a rotation retroactively expires every old artefact; --at turns it back ... needs a trusted timestamp." Base 173282c: no match for timestamp, integratedTime or rfc3161; verifyWith(envelope, trust, at = Date.now()) (src/cli.mjs:119) judges not_after against the verify-time clock or --at. verifyWith judges not_after against a trusted signing time when the envelope carries one: a Sigstore bundle beside it whose verified timestamp (Rekor integratedTime or an RFC 3161 token) @sigstore/verify checks. Without one, the time is the verifier's clock as now. --at stays but is reported as an assertion by the verifier, never as a trusted time; verify --json gains time: {value, source: rekor | rfc3161 | clock | asserted}. A rotation's not_after then expires only what was signed after it. Revocation is unchanged: a revoked key fails at any time. @sigstore/verify moves from devDependencies to optionalDependencies, loaded on first use; without it an envelope that carries a bundle exits 2 AGENTKEY_SIGSTORE_UNAVAILABLE and is never judged by the clock in silence. The timestamped fixtures come from a real Rekor or TSA response recorded once, with its source named; a timestamp agentkey makes for itself does not count.

criteria.statement: signed and timestamped before not_after verifies after it; without the timestamp exits 2 expired; a timestamp after not_after exits 2; a bundle whose timestamp does not verify exits 1; --at is reported as source asserted; a revoked key fails whatever the time

tasks.title: A plain install fetches no Sigstore package; keyless signing works once @sigstore/sign is installed
tasks.description: Owner decision of 2026-10-17 for HV-12 (option (b)): agentkey 0.1.1. package.json moves @sigstore/sign 3.1.0 from optionalDependencies to peerDependencies, with peerDependenciesMeta { "@sigstore/sign": { "optional": true } }, so npm does not install it on its own. It is also added to devDependencies at 3.1.0, so agentkey's own suite and its lockfile keep it: @sigstore/verify does not bring it, and the keyless tests (sigstore_absent.test.mjs, the interop test) need it installed. dependencies and optionalDependencies are empty, and the version is 0.1.1. package-lock.json is regenerated to match in the same commit (npm install --package-lock-only --ignore-scripts, empty user config); because @sigstore/sign is a devDependency it keeps node_modules/@sigstore/sign with integrity, so AK-LOCK-AC02's check holds. signKeyless keeps its lazy load and AGENTKEY_SIGSTORE_UNAVAILABLE; the message names the command that adds it (npm install @sigstore/sign@3.1.0). README.md:220 and the comment at src/sigstore.mjs:2-3 say 'optional peer dependency' and give that command. CHANGELOG has an Unreleased line. Red on base: the manifest has the optional dependency, and the install fetches @sigstore/sign. The test installs with --prefer-offline, not --offline: npm skips an optional dependency that fails to fetch, so an offline install would leave the directory empty on base and the red would be false. AK-06-VER-AC01 greps package.json for "version": "0.1.0", which stops matching at 0.1.1. That is expected: 0.1.0 is the released version that task recorded, the CHANGELOG heading AK-06-VER-AC02 checks stays, and a later re-verify of AK-06-VER that fails only that grep is not a regression. The npm release of 0.1.1 is the owner's step, and HV-12's re-pin to 0.1.1 follows it.

criteria.statement: the package declares no dependency or optional dependency and @sigstore/sign as an optional peer; installing the packed tarball into a scratch project (npm install --prefer-offline --ignore-scripts) leaves no node_modules/@sigstore; after npm install @sigstore/sign@3.1.0 into that project, signKeyless called with no identityToken throws exactly AGENTKEY_SIGSTORE_NO_TOKEN, in a child whose env has SIGSTORE_ID_TOKEN, ACTIONS_ID_TOKEN_REQUEST_URL and ACTIONS_ID_TOKEN_REQUEST_TOKEN removed, so it stops at src/sigstore.mjs:21-27 before anything is sent, on any runner including CI. The test makes its own empty npm user config file and passes it to both installs as NPM_CONFIG_USERCONFIG, never the home one, and gives each install its own timeout
